title: Feedback effect on input and output impedance

sections.heading: The idea
sections.body_md:
Feedback changes the impedances an amplifier presents. How depends on how it **samples** the output and how it **mixes** the feedback into the input.

For the classic voltage amplifier (series mixing at the input, shunt sampling at the output), the input source only has to supply the tiny error voltage, so the input impedance is multiplied by \(1 + T\). At the output, any load-induced voltage change is seen and corrected by the loop, so the output impedance is divided by \(1 + T\). The rule of thumb: series connections multiply impedance by \(1 + T\), shunt connections divide it. Voltage feedback makes a voltage amplifier more ideal at both ports.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
Series input, shunt output (voltage amplifier):
\[ Z_{in,fb} = R_{in}(1 + Af), \qquad Z_{out,fb} = \frac{R_{out}}{1 + Af} \]
Shunt input: \(Z_{in,fb} = \dfrac{R_{in}}{1 + Af}\). Series output (current sampling): \(Z_{out,fb} = R_{out}(1 + Af)\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
An op-amp with \(R_{in} = 500\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\), \(R_{out} = 100\ \Omega\) and \(A = 5\times10^4\) is used as a non-inverting amplifier with gain 10 (\(f = 0.1\)), so \(Af = 5000\).
\[ Z_{in,fb} \approx 500\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\times5001 \approx 2.5\ \mathrm{G\Omega} \]
\[ Z_{out,fb} \approx \frac{100}{5001} \approx 20\ \mathrm{m\Omega} \]

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
- Applying the same \(1 + T\) rule in the same direction to both ports.
- Forgetting that the result also depends on \(T\) falling with frequency.
- Confusing input resistance of the inverting amplifier (\(\approx R_1\)) with the op-amp's own input resistance.
- Using \(A\) instead of \(Af\).

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: These impedance rules explain why op-amp circuits make good buffers and why some feedback topologies suit current-output or current-input applications.
